inline.s: Good friends! Maha-Prajna-Paramita is Sanskrit; in the speech of Tang it is great wisdom reaching the other shore. This must be practiced with the mind, not spoken with the mouth. To speak it with the mouth while not practicing it with the mind is like illusion, like transformation, like dew, like lightning; but to speak it with the mouth and practice it with the mind is for mind and mouth to be in accord. The fundamental nature is the Buddha; apart from the nature there is no other Buddha.

What is called maha? Maha is great. The capacity of the mind is vast, like empty space, with no bounds, no square or round, no great or small, no blue, yellow, red or white, no above or below, no long or short, no anger or joy, no right or wrong, no good or evil, no head or tail.
The lands of all Buddhas are alike empty space. The wondrous nature of people is fundamentally empty, and not a single dharma can be obtained. The true emptiness of the self-nature is likewise.

Good friends! Do not, on hearing me speak of emptiness, then attach to emptiness. Above all do not attach to emptiness! If one empties the mind and sits in stillness, one attaches to the emptiness of indeterminacy.

Good friends! The emptiness of the world can hold all the forms of things — the sun, moon, stars and constellations, the mountains, rivers and the great earth, springs, sources, streams and valleys, grass and trees and thickets, evil men and good men, evil dharmas and good dharmas, heavens and hells, all the great seas, all the Sumeru mountains — all are within the emptiness. The emptiness of the nature of people is likewise.

Good friends! That the self-nature can contain all dharmas is the great — all dharmas are within the nature of all people. If one sees both the evil and the good of all people, taking none up and rejecting none, and is not defiled by them, having a mind like empty space, this is called great; therefore it is called maha.

Good friends! The deluded speak with the mouth; the wise practice with the mind. There are also the deluded who empty the mind and sit in stillness, thinking of nothing at all, and call themselves great; with this kind of people one cannot speak, because of their wrong views.

Good friends! The vast capacity of the mind pervades the whole Dharma-realm. In function it is clearly distinct, and in responding it knows all things. All is one, and one is all. Going and coming freely, the mind-substance without obstruction — this is prajna.

Good friends! All prajna wisdom is born from the self-nature and does not enter from without; do not misdirect your intention. This is the self-use of the true nature, the one real being all real. The vast matter of the mind does not walk the small path. Do not all day speak of emptiness with the mouth, while within the mind you do not practice this practice — that is like a common man calling himself a king, which can never be obtained, and such a one is not my disciple.

Good friends! What is called prajna? Prajna, in the language of Tang, is wisdom. In every place and at every time, thought after thought without delusion, ever practicing wisdom — this is the practice of prajna. In a single thought of delusion prajna is cut off; in a single thought of wisdom prajna is born. Worldly people, deluded and confused, do not see prajna; they speak of prajna with the mouth, while the mind is ever deluded, and they constantly say they cultivate prajna, thought after thought speaking of emptiness, yet not knowing the true emptiness. Prajna has no form or mark; the wisdom mind itself is it. If one understands it thus, it is called prajna wisdom.

What is called paramita? This is a word of the western regions; in the speech of Tang it means reaching the other shore, understanding the meaning of leaving birth and death. When one attaches to objects, birth and death arise, as water has waves — this is called this shore; when apart from objects there is no birth and death, as water flows ever through — this is called the other shore. Hence it is named paramita.

Good friends! When the deluded recite with the mouth, at the time of recitation there is falsehood and wrongness. If thought after thought one practices it, this is called the true nature. One who awakens to this method is in the prajna Dharma; one who practices this practice is in the prajna practice. Not to practice — that is the ordinary man; in a single thought of practice, one's own body is equal to the Buddha.

Good friends! The ordinary man is the Buddha; affliction is bodhi. With a former thought deluded, one is the ordinary man; with a later thought awakened, one is a Buddha. With a former thought attached to objects, there is affliction; with a later thought apart from objects, there is bodhi.
Good friends!
Maha-prajna-paramita, most honored, highest, first;
No abiding, no going, no coming — from it the Buddhas of three times burst.

One should use great wisdom to break through the five aggregates, affliction and the dust of toil. Cultivating thus, one is certain to accomplish the Buddha-way, transforming the three poisons into precepts, concentration and wisdom.

Good friends! In this Dharma-gate of mine, from one prajna are born eighty-four thousand wisdoms. Why? Because worldly people have eighty-four thousand kinds of dust and toil. If there were no dust and toil, wisdom would ever appear and never leave the self-nature. One who awakens to this method is without thought, without recollection, without attachment. Not giving rise to falsehood and deceit, and using one's own true-tathata nature, with wisdom contemplating and illuminating, taking nothing up and rejecting nothing among all dharmas — this is seeing the nature and accomplishing the Buddha-way.

Good friends! If you wish to enter the profound Dharma-realm and the samadhi of prajna, you must cultivate the practice of prajna. Holding and reciting the Diamond Prajna Sutra, one sees the nature. You should know that the merit of this sutra is immeasurable and boundless; the sutra itself clearly praises it, and it cannot be fully spoken. This Dharma-gate is the supreme vehicle, spoken for the greatly wise, spoken for those of superior faculties; those of small wisdom and small faculties, hearing it, give rise to unbelief in their hearts.

Why? For example, when a dragon of heaven rains upon Jambudvipa, the cities and villages are all carried off, as the leaves of the jujube are swept along; but if it rains upon the great sea, it neither increases nor diminishes. If a man of the Great Vehicle, if a man of the supreme vehicle, hears the Diamond Sutra and his mind opens in understanding, he knows that the fundamental nature itself possesses prajna wisdom, and because he constantly contemplates with his own wisdom, he does not rely on words. For example, the rain does not come out of the sky itself; it is the dragon's power that stirs it up, that all sentient beings, all plants and trees, the sentient and the insentient alike, may all be moistened, while the hundred rivers and streams all flow into the great sea and become one body. The prajna wisdom of the fundamental nature of sentient beings is likewise.

Good friends! When those of small faculties hear this Sudden Teaching, it is like the plants and trees of small root: if caught in a great rain, they are all toppled over and cannot grow. Those of small faculties are likewise — though they originally have prajna wisdom with no difference from the greatly wise, why do they not awaken on hearing the Dharma? Because of the heavy obstruction of wrong views and the deep roots of affliction, like a great cloud covering the sun; without the wind to blow it away, the sunlight does not appear.

The wisdom of prajna has no great or small, because the self-minds of all beings differ in delusion and awakening. A deluded mind seeing outward, cultivating and seeking the Buddha, not yet awakened to the self-nature — this is small faculties. But if one is awakened to the Sudden Teaching, not holding to outward practice, and within one's own mind always raises right views, so that affliction and the dust of toil can never defile it — this is seeing the nature.

Good friends! Not dwelling within or without, going and coming freely, able to remove the clinging mind and penetrate without obstruction — one who cultivates this practice is in no way different from the Prajna Sutra.

Good friends! All sutras and all written texts — the two vehicles, the twelve divisions of the canon — are all established for people, depending on the nature of wisdom, and only then can they be set up. If there were no worldly people, all the myriad dharmas would originally not exist. Therefore know that the myriad dharmas are originally established by people, and all scriptures are spoken because of people. Because among people there are the dull and the wise, the dull are the small men and the wise the great men. The dull ask the wise, and the wise speak the Dharma for the dull; the dull, suddenly awakening, understanding and opening their minds, are no different from the wise.

Good friends! Without awakening, the Buddha is a sentient being; with a single thought of awakening, the sentient being is a Buddha. Therefore know that all the myriad dharmas are within your own mind — why not from your own mind suddenly see the true-tathata fundamental nature? The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Precepts says: "My own fundamental self-nature is pure; if you know your own mind and see the nature, all accomplish the Buddha-way." The Vimalakirti Sutra says: "Instantly it becomes all at once clear, and the original mind is regained."

Good friends! At the place of the Master Ren (Hongren), as soon as I heard a single phrase I awakened, and suddenly saw the true-tathata fundamental nature. Therefore I have spread this teaching abroad, so that those who study the Way may suddenly awaken to bodhi. Each of you contemplate your own mind and see your own fundamental nature.

If you cannot awaken yourselves, you must seek a great good friend, one who understands the Dharma of the supreme vehicle, to point directly to the right path. Such a good friend has a great relation — namely, to guide and transform so that one sees the nature; all good dharmas are able to be set moving because of the good friend. The Buddhas of the three times and the twelve divisions of the canon are originally complete within the nature of people. If one cannot awaken oneself, one must seek a good friend to point and show, and only then see; but if one awakens oneself, one need not seek outside. If one persists in holding that one must rely on a good friend outside and hopes to gain liberation thereby, there is no such principle. Why? Because within one's own mind there is a good friend who makes one aware and self-awakened. If one has given rise to wrong confusion and inverted, false thoughts, though an outward good friend can teach, he cannot save. But if one sets going the true, right prajna contemplation, in an instant all false thoughts are extinguished; if one recognizes the self-nature, in a single awakening one reaches the Buddha-ground.

Good friends! Contemplating with wisdom, within and without illumined and clear, one knows one's own fundamental mind. If you know the fundamental mind, you are fundamentally liberated. If you attain liberation, that is the samadhi of prajna, and that is "no-thought."

What is called no-thought? If, seeing all dharmas, the mind is not defiled by them, this is no-thought. In function it pervades every place, yet is not attached to any place. Only purify the fundamental mind, so that the six consciousnesses issue from the six gates, and amid the six objects there is no defilement and no mixing, going and coming freely, in universal function without obstruction — this is the samadhi of prajna, liberation at ease, called the practice of no-thought. If one thinks of nothing whatever, and causes thought to be cut off, that is Dharma-bondage, and is called a one-sided view.

Good friends! One who awakens to the no-thought Dharma penetrates all dharmas; one who awakens to the no-thought Dharma sees the realm of all Buddhas; one who awakens to the no-thought Dharma reaches the stage of Buddhahood.

Good friends! Among my descendants, those who obtain my Dharma, if they bring this Sudden Teaching gate, with those of like views and like practice, and make the vow to hold it as they would serve the Buddha, and to the end of life do not retreat — they will surely enter the sage's stage. But one must transmit the silent, secret transmission handed down from above, and must not conceal the right Dharma. If, with those of unlike views and unlike practice, in another teaching, one must not transmit it; for that would harm those former men, and in the end be of no benefit. I fear that the foolish, not understanding, might slander this Dharma-gate, and for a hundred eons and a thousand lives cut off the Buddha-seed nature.

Good friends! I have a "Verse of the Formless"; let each of you take it up and recite it, whether at home or in the monastery, and cultivate only in accord with it. If you do not cultivate yourselves and merely remember my words, it is of no benefit. Hear my verse:
Speech relates and mind relates, as the sun in the void abides; To pass on the seeing-nature Dharma, come forth and break the false guides.
The Dharma has no sudden or gradual; delusion and awakening have slow and fast. This gate of seeing the nature alone, the foolish cannot fully know.
Speech, though it is a thousand kinds, accords with principle and returns to one. In the dark house of affliction, one must ever raise the sun of wisdom.
When wrong comes, affliction arrives; when right comes, affliction is removed. Using neither wrong nor right, purity reaches the utterly without remainder.
Bodhi is the self-nature; to stir the mind is falsehood. The pure mind is amid falsehood; being right, there are no three hindrances.
If worldly people cultivate the Way, all things are no hindrance. Constantly seeing one's own faults, one is in accord with the Way.
Each class of form has its own Way, and they do not hinder or trouble one another. To leave the Way and seek another Way, to the end of life one will not see the Way.
Wave upon wave one passes a whole life, and in the end only regrets. If you would see the true Way, conduct that is upright is itself the Way.
If one has no mind for the Way, walking in darkness one does not see the Way. If one is a true cultivator of the Way, one does not see the faults of the world.
If you see the wrongs of others, your own wrong is the greater. Though another is wrong and I am not, when I am wrong I have a fault myself.
Only remove the mind of fault, and strike away affliction. Being unconcerned with hate and love, stretch out your two legs and lie down.
If you would transform others, you must yourself have expedient means. Do not let them have doubt; this is the self-nature revealing.
The Buddha-Dharma is in the world; it does not leave the worldly awakening. To seek bodhi apart from the world is exactly like seeking a rabbit's horn.
Right view is called transcendent; wrong view is called worldly. When wrong and right are both struck away, the bodhi nature is manifest.
This verse is the Sudden Teaching, also called the great Dharma-boat. The deluded hear it through many eons; the awakened in an instant.

The Master again said: Now, preaching this Sudden Teaching at the Great Brahma temple, I universally vow that sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, at these very words, see the nature and become Buddha.

At that time the Prefect Wei, with the officials and the clergy and lay alike, hearing what the Master said, none but awakened. All at once they made obeisance, and all lamented with joy, "Excellent! Who would have thought that in Lingnan a Buddha had appeared in the world!"

blocks.text: Third, the Chapter of Resolving Doubts

inline.s: One day the Prefect Wei held a great assembly feast for the Master. When the meal was done, the Prefect requested the Master to ascend the seat, and with the officials, scholars and commoners, of solemn countenance, made obeisance again and again, then asked, "Your disciple has heard the Master preach the Dharma, and it is truly inconceivable. Now I have a small doubt, and I beg the great compassion to explain it especially for me." The Master said, "If you have a doubt, ask at once; I will speak it for you."

The Prefect said, "What the Master preaches — is it not the fundamental implication of the Great Master Bodhidharma?" The Master said, "It is." The Prefect said, "Your disciple has heard that when Bodhidharma first taught Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor asked: 'I have all my life built temples, ordained monks, given alms and set up feasts; what merit have I gained?' Bodhidharma said: 'There is in truth no merit.' Your disciple has not yet penetrated this principle, and begs the Master to explain it."
